title: Aditi Paudel, 17, Becomes Japan's First Literacy Ambassador
excerpt: The Nepali-origin high school senior in Tokyo has been appointed by the World Literacy Foundation, becoming the first ambassador from Japan in the program's 12-year history.
body:
• Aditi Paudel, a 17-year-old high school senior of Nepali origin living in Tokyo, has been appointed Japan's first literacy ambassador by the Australia-based World Literacy Foundation.
  • Born in Japan and raised in Nepal during early childhood, Paudel navigated multiple languages and scripts before returning to Tokyo for third grade, where she had to relearn Japanese.
  • The World Literacy Foundation's ambassador program spans roughly 900 young people aged 16 to 25 across 101 countries, and this is the first time an ambassador has been appointed from Japan in its 12-year history.
  • Paudel plans to work with children with disabilities and partner with the Shanti Volunteer Association to collect and send books to Asian countries with lower literacy rates, including Nepal.

A First for Japan

Aditi Paudel was reading Devanagari script in preschool, a skill inherited from afternoons with her grandfather and his Nepali newspaper. A decade later, the 17-year-old high school senior in Tokyo has been named Japan's first literacy ambassador by the World Literacy Foundation, a global nonprofit based in Australia.

https://x.com/timesofindia/status/2094726970684887238

The appointment marks the first time in the program's 12-year history that an ambassador has been selected from Japan. The foundation's network now includes roughly 900 young advocates aged 16 to 25 across 101 countries.

"Her curiosity about English shaped thoughtful advocacy, strengthening the program's global voice and cultural reach."

— Andrew Kay, CEO, World Literacy Foundation

Between Scripts and Continents

Paudel was born in Japan to Nepali parents but spent her early childhood in Nepal, where her grandfather's gift of a newspaper became her earliest reading memory. She returned to Japan for third grade and faced the challenge of relearning Japanese, a language she had lost during her years away.

Her father filled their home with books, and Paudel gravitated toward fantasy fiction — Enid Blyton's "The Wishing-Chair" was an early favourite. It was Malala Yousafzai's "I Am Malala" that shifted her focus toward female empowerment and access to education, themes that now anchor her advocacy work.

The experience of moving between Nepali, Japanese, and English — each with its own script and cultural framework — gave Paudel an acute understanding of how language shapes opportunity. Japan's literacy rate sits at roughly 99 percent, but Nepal's hovers around 76 percent, with a significant gender gap: 84 percent for men and 69 percent for women.

What She Plans to Do

Paudel's agenda as ambassador extends beyond symbolic recognition. She intends to work with children with disabilities in Japan, a demographic that often faces barriers to literacy programs designed for mainstream learners.

She also plans to partner with the Shanti Volunteer Association, a Japanese NGO, to collect and distribute books to countries across Asia with lower literacy rates, including her family's homeland of Nepal.

"Her leadership, passion for literacy, and commitment to empowering young people in Japan are truly inspiring."

— Andrew Kay, CEO, World Literacy Foundation

A South Asian Story Abroad

Paudel's story resonates beyond Japan's borders. It reflects a pattern familiar across the South Asian diaspora: young people navigating multiple languages, cultural identities, and expectations while channelling those experiences into global impact.

Her commitment to supporting literacy in Nepal connects to a broader tradition of diaspora giving-back, where second-generation South Asians use their positions abroad to address gaps in their countries of origin. In Paudel's case, the gap is not economic but educational — the difference between a country where nearly everyone can read and one where a third of women cannot.

At 17, she is one of the youngest ambassadors in the foundation's network, and the first to represent a country where illiteracy is statistically rare but where linguistic diversity and disability inclusion remain works in progress.
